I can answer that question. Solar power succeeds well when it is not based on silicon. Silicon is the go-to for cheap and reliable semiconductors. Doping wafers of silicon turns it into an extrinsic semiconductor, a p-n junction, allowing the photovoltaic effect to have a bigger impact in the creation of a forward bias. Creating p-n junctions from other materials is technically straightforward. The cost comes with the creation and doping of alloys (as opposed to straight up singular matter). Alloy creation is critical for fine control of band characteristics, which permit these special junctions to increase amount of the forward bias applied compared to semiconductors based on singular materials, and the rate of the injection of carriers.

Compared to silicon, these alloys are not cheap to produce, but as new and refining of production methods will bring these costs down. It is merely a question of return-of-investment, as solar cells are delicate, initial costs are high, and can burn out like an overworked diode eventually (this is improving, silicon-based cells currently have a life of an estimated 60 years).

Oil, coal, and natural gases on the other hand, can be refined (and even reclaimed, in some cases) to a different numbers of fuels, and other useful carbon-based products. The energy can be stored without batteries or capacitor banks, and combusted when needed. With current infrastructure in place, fossil has a lower initial cost to burn, and engines today are reasonably efficient. This does come at a cost at waste and maintenance costs from production and use which is notably higher then solar.

Energy storage is often omitted when it comes to these arguments. Solar and wind utilities are created today to supplement other utilities. In the scenario where we are more significantly solar dependent, we would need electrical storage facilities, which produced today, would significantly raise costs to ludicrous. We have a long way to go in this field.

Even with the government "re-balancing" the scales, solar still can not compete at the moment. Since I'm on the topic, the government also has a hand in helping oil: by encouraging 10-15% of corn based ethanol (corn is also subsidised) in conventional blends, they made costs cheaper at the expense of fuel efficiency.
